Cash now or payments later: compare present value without losing the receipt calendar

Compare an immediate lump sum with a finite annual payment stream, discount each receipt to the same date, and distinguish eventual totals from the cash available for current bills.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Put an upfront receipt and a dated payment stream on the same valuation date

Interactive planning lab

Present value of the dated payments$51,953.72
Present value less upfront alternative$1,953.72
Total payments before discounting$60,000

All amounts, dates and discount rates are independently entered hypothetical assumptions. The alternatives are mutually exclusive receipts: the upfront amount is received at time zero, while the equal annual payments occur at first-payment year plus successive whole years. Year 0 means an immediate first payment. Enter spendable amounts on a consistent tax and cost basis; no tax calculation is made. Every scheduled payment is assumed paid in full on its stated date. The effective annual discount rate converts amounts to time-zero value and is not an available investment yield, inflation estimate or probability adjustment. Cumulative receipt totals exclude reinvestment, spending and borrowing. Present value is an analytical measure, not extra money available in the bank. Credit risk, benefit eligibility, life contingencies, assignment rights and actual contract terms are outside this calculation.

The central idea

An eventual payment total, its present value and the amount available today answer different questions. Keep all three beside the actual receipt dates.

01

Write down the receipts before choosing a valuation method

Suppose a household can receive CAD 50,000 immediately or CAD 12,000 once a year for five years, with the first payment one year from now. The second option totals CAD 60,000. That larger numeral alone does not tell us whether it is more valuable today or whether it can meet a bill due next month.

The alternatives have different dates as well as different totals. An immediate receipt can be assigned to a current need. A future receipt is assumed to arrive only on its stated date. This guide keeps a cash calendar beside a present-value comparison so the valuation does not erase that distinction.

The tool assumes that the alternatives are mutually exclusive and every scheduled payment is made in full. Enter amounts on the same spendable basis. It does not estimate taxes, establish a right to choose a different payment form, or value a life-contingent pension. A real contract must first identify what is payable, when it is payable and under what conditions.

02

Convert each payment to the same date exactly once

The OpenStax discussion of annuities explains how a stream of fixed payments can be valued by discounting each receipt. Its cash-flow timing chapter also shows why a dated timeline matters when amounts occur in different periods. This guide applies that method to an independently authored example.

A payment due in year t has a time-zero value of payment ÷ (1 + effective annual discount rate)t. The immediate amount is already at time zero, so it is not discounted for another year. A payment received now likewise has an exponent of zero.

The selected discount rate is a valuation assumption. It does not guarantee that the household can earn that rate, and it does not automatically incorporate tax, default risk or inflation. Choosing a rate appropriate to an actual decision needs a separate assessment of its cash flows and alternatives; this illustration does not supply a market quote.

Keep the analytical discount rate separate from a price-year conversion. Expressing a future receipt in constant purchasing power requires a specified inflation path. Comparing its value with an alternative use of money requires a consistent valuation assumption. If amounts have already been converted to constant-price dollars, applying a rate on a different price basis can combine inconsistent units. This tool uses payment-year dollars, a discount rate on that basis and no second inflation conversion.

03

Explain the default result through individual discounted receipts

At a hypothetical 5% effective annual discount rate, the first CAD 12,000 payment has a present value of approximately CAD 11,428.57. The fifth payment has a present value of approximately CAD 9,402.31 because its receipt is five years away.

Adding all five discounted payments produces about CAD 51,953.72. Subtracting the immediate CAD 50,000 alternative leaves a positive valuation difference of about CAD 1,953.72. The waterfall shows each discounted payment and the final subtraction, so the result can be traced without treating the entire CAD 60,000 as money received today.

This is an arithmetic comparison under the stated assumptions. It does not create CAD 51,953.72 of accessible cash, nor does it establish that borrowing against future receipts would be available or inexpensive. Discounting a payment to time zero and then deducting an additional generic “waiting cost” would also count the same selected time-value assumption twice unless that cost represents a separate identified cash flow.

04

Keep the cumulative receipt line separate from an investment account

The cumulative chart begins with CAD 50,000 received under the upfront alternative and zero received under the default delayed alternative. The latter rises by CAD 12,000 at each annual receipt. It reaches CAD 60,000 after the fifth payment.

No return is earned in that chart. The upfront line stays at CAD 50,000 because it records total receipts, rather than a growing investment. Spending is also absent, so neither line is a forecast of the bank balance remaining after bills. A household that spends an immediate receipt will not still own all of it simply because its cumulative-receipts line stays level.

A larger eventual receipt total can coexist with a lower present value. At an 8% discount rate, the same five payments are worth about CAD 47,912.52 today, below the CAD 50,000 alternative. The receipt dates and total have not changed; the analytical rate used to compare them has. The matrix makes that sensitivity visible.

05

Shift the whole payment calendar instead of adding an unexplained adjustment

The first-payment control can move the equal stream while retaining its size and count. With five payments starting in year zero, the dates are zero through four. Starting in year one gives dates one through five. Starting in year three gives dates three through seven.

At 5%, moving the default stream two years later reduces its present value from CAD 51,953.72 to about CAD 47,123.56. This equals the original present value divided by 1.05 squared. The undiscounted total remains CAD 60,000 because no payment has been removed or reduced.

At a zero discount rate, the model values every dated dollar equally, so the timing rows show the same difference for a given total. That does not eliminate a household’s need for cash before a payment arrives. It shows the consequence of using zero as the analytical rate. The schedule still identifies those earlier periods without receipts.

06

Check the current spending need and payment conditions separately

A household may prefer a regular receipt pattern for budgeting, or need more money immediately for a known obligation. Those practical needs should be specified directly. They are not automatically settled by the sign of a present-value difference.

For example, a CAD 15,000 bill due now cannot be paid from the first default installment one year later. Funding that bill from existing savings changes how much of those savings remains for other needs. Borrowing instead introduces its own proceeds, interest and repayment dates. Neither action is assumed in this receipt-only comparison.

Before applying the method to an actual offer, check payment certainty, gross versus net amounts, fees, any indexing, transfer restrictions and the consequences of a recipient’s death. A finite stream assumed fully payable differs from a payment that depends on continued survival or another condition. Record those terms alongside the timeline, then value the resulting cash flows on a consistent date. The charts explain the method while leaving those contract-specific facts to the actual evidence.
